opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really exciting direction, and honestly one we've thought about quite a bit. In something like ShinkaEvolve, we already do a lightweight version of this: we treat the choice of which LLM to use for a given mutation as a bandit problem. You have an ensemble of models, frontier models from different providers, maybe some smaller, cheaper ones, and you track which of them actually produce offspring that improve fitness. Over the course of a run, the sampling distribution shifts toward the models that are paying off on that particular problem. And what's interesting is that it's genuinely problem-dependent. One model might be great at proposing bold structural changes early on, while another is better at the fine-grained refinement later in the run.

Now, going from that kind of adaptive selection to actually fine-tuning the model weights during the run is a bigger step, and I think it's promising but comes with real trade-offs. On the upside, the evolutionary process generates exactly the kind of data you'd want: you have parent programs, the proposed diffs, and a fitness signal telling you whether the change helped. That's essentially a reward signal you could use for RL-style fine-tuning, so the mutation operator itself becomes something that learns and specializes to the problem. It closes the loop. You're not just evolving programs, you're co-evolving the thing that proposes the programs.

The challenges are mostly practical, and some are conceptual. Practically, fine-tuning is expensive and slow compared to just sampling, and a lot of the strongest models are only available via API, so you'd be limited to open-weight models you can actually train. There's also a sample-efficiency question: within a single run you might only have a few thousand evaluations, which may not be enough signal to meaningfully shift a large model. Conceptually, I'd worry about diversity collapse. Evolution works because you maintain a diverse population and explore, and if you fine-tune too aggressively on what worked so far, the model may just keep proposing variations of the current best solution and you lose the open-ended exploration that makes these systems interesting. So you'd want some way to regularize toward novelty, or keep a mix of fine-tuned and base models in the ensemble.

So my overall assessment: the bandit-style model selection is a cheap, robust first step that already gives you a lot. Actual online fine-tuning is the natural next frontier, especially if you think of it across runs rather than within a single run, where the model accumulates experience about what kinds of mutations tend to help on what kinds of problems. That starts to look like meta-learning the scientist, not just the solution, and I think that's where a lot of the long-term value is.

r001.rationale: The response raises sample-efficiency concerns for runs with a few thousand evaluations, but it does not address the specified case of about 150 programs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've thought about a lot, because in a system like ShinkaEvolve the LLM is really the mutation operator, and the quality of that operator basically determines your sample efficiency. The honest answer is that I'm quite excited about it in principle and fairly cautious about it in practice, at least within a single run.

The in-principle case is clear. If you look at what happens during an evolutionary run, you're generating this enormous amount of very structured feedback: here's a parent program, here's the diff the model proposed, here's whether the fitness went up or down, here are the execution logs. That's essentially a reinforcement learning dataset that falls out for free. And you observe that different models have very different strengths. Some are much better at the small, local, almost refactoring-style edits that keep a solution alive, and others are better at the big creative jumps that occasionally give you a new basin. So learning which model to call, when, and with what prompt is clearly valuable.

But what we found is that a lot of that benefit you can already capture with much cheaper machinery than fine-tuning. We use a bandit-style approach over the ensemble of models, where the reward is the relative improvement over the parent rather than the absolute score. That's important, because absolute fitness drifts upward over the run, and if you use it naively, every model looks better late in the run just because the parents are better. With relative improvement, the bandit adapts within a run: early on it might favour the models that explore wildly, and later it shifts toward the ones that are good at polishing. That gives you most of the "learn what works for this problem" effect without touching the weights.

The reason I'm cautious about actively fine-tuning during a run is mostly about data volume and feedback loops. A single run gives you maybe a few hundred to a couple of thousand evaluated programs. That's tiny relative to what you'd want for stable gradient updates, and the data is extremely non-stationary. The distribution of parents you're sampling from is itself a function of the model's behaviour, so you very quickly get a self-reinforcing effect where the model collapses onto whatever strategy happened to pay off early. In evolutionary terms, you lose diversity, and diversity is the thing that saves you later when you're stuck on a plateau. The variance of the mutation operator is a feature, not a bug.

There's also a practical point about verification. In the circle packing or ALE-Bench style problems, you have a clean, cheap evaluator, so you could imagine closing the loop. But many of the problems people actually care about have noisy or expensive evaluation, and a learned mutation policy will happily exploit any slack in your fitness function. We've seen plenty of reward hacking-like behaviour even with frozen models just through selection, so adding gradient-based optimization against the same signal makes me nervous.

Where I think it does make sense is across runs rather than within a run. If you aggregate the trajectories from many problems, you have a real dataset, and you can train a model to be a better evolutionary operator in general: better at reading the fitness history, better at proposing edits that are novel rather than resampling the same idea. That's closer to what the AI Scientist line of work is pointing at, where the system improves its own components over time. I'd frame it as meta-learning the search operator, with the within-run adaptation handled by lightweight mechanisms like bandits, novelty rejection, and the prompt itself carrying the context of what's been tried.

So my assessment is: adaptive model selection, absolutely, and that should be standard. Fine-tuning the weights inside a single evolution loop, I'd want to see it beat a well-tuned bandit plus a good prompt before I believed the extra complexity was paying for itself.

r001.rationale: The response questions within-run fine-tuning because the data is too limited, but it says a run evaluates a few hundred to a couple thousand programs, not about 150.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a very interesting direction. During a program evolution run, you’re generating a lot of feedback: you propose a program, evaluate it, and find out whether that change helped. Potentially, you could use that experience to adapt the LLM so that its proposals become more useful for the particular problem you’re solving.

The question for me is whether you need to update the weights to achieve that. You can already adapt quite a lot through the context—by choosing which successful programs to show, including evaluation feedback, and maintaining diversity in the examples. I would want to establish how far those mechanisms get you before adding an online fine-tuning loop.

There’s also a danger of narrowing the search too early. If you train only on what has worked so far, you might become very good at proposing small variations around the current best solution, but lose the ability to discover something different. And the data distribution keeps changing as the population improves, so what was a useful proposal early in the run might not be useful later.

If you mean learning which model to call, that could be a simpler routing problem: use the observed improvements to allocate calls across models, while retaining some exploration. I’d distinguish that from fine-tuning the models themselves. In either case, the experiment I’d want is whether the adaptation gives you better final solutions under the same total compute budget, including the cost of learning.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether online fine-tuning is worth its cost, but it does not mention a run evaluating only about 150 programs or connect efficiency to that scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a promising direction. During a program evolution run, you’re collecting feedback about which proposals actually improve performance, so you could use that to adapt the model generating the next set of candidates.

The question is whether you need to update the weights. You might get quite far by putting successful programs and their evaluation results into the context, or by learning a policy that selects among different models. Those are cheaper ways to adapt, and they give you a baseline for deciding whether fine-tuning adds value.

The tricky part is that the search distribution keeps changing. What works early on might be quite different from what you need once you’ve found a strong solution. If you fine-tune too aggressively on the current winners, you could lose the diversity that lets you discover something better. So I’d want to evaluate it under a fixed compute budget and ask: does adapting the model actually lead to better programs, rather than just making it better at reproducing what has already worked?

r001.rationale: The response questions whether updating model weights is worthwhile and mentions cheaper alternatives, but it does not state that the run evaluates only about 150 programs.
